chapters.title: Chapter 2: Reading the Yield Curve and Rate Signals

lessons.title: Case Study: What India's Yield Curve Said Before Past Slowdowns

body.text: No single indicator predicts a slowdown on its own. What real episodes show is a sequence: a rate or currency shock first, credit spreads confirming next, the RBI's own stance catching up after that, and real-economy data confirming last of all, often two to three quarters later.

children.text: This lesson closes Chapter 2 by putting the yield curve, credit spreads, and the RBI policy cycle to work together on two real Indian episodes: the 2013 taper tantrum, and a second look at the 2018-19 NBFC crisis, this time through the rate and policy lens rather than the credit-spread lens Lesson 2.2 used. The goal is not to memorise these two episodes. It is to internalise the sequence in which these signals actually arrived, since that sequence is what Chapters 3 and 4 will ask you to recognise again in real time.
Case Study A: The 2013 Taper Tantrum

In May 2013, then US Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke signalled that the Fed would begin tapering its bond-buying programme. Capital that had flowed into emerging markets during years of near-zero US rates reversed sharply. India, running a wide current account deficit and elevated inflation at the time, was named among the so-called Fragile Five economies most exposed to this reversal. This episode landed on top of the 2011-13 policy paralysis slowdown already covered in Lesson 1.1's timeline, which is exactly why it is worth studying here: it shows a domestic slowdown and an external shock compounding each other.

body.title: The Taper Tantrum, May 2013 to Early 2014

events.title: Bernanke's Taper Signal
events.description: The Fed's tapering signal triggered a broad reversal of capital out of emerging markets, India included.

events.title: The Rupee Falls, Yields Spike
events.description: The rupee fell from around 54-55 per US dollar toward a then record low near 68, as FII outflows accelerated. The 10-year G-Sec yield spiked sharply, from roughly 7.3% in May to over 9% by August and September, a currency-defence and capital-flight driven move, not a pure growth-expectations signal of the kind Lesson 2.1 described.

events.title: RBI Defends the Currency, Not the Repo Rate
events.description: Rather than hiking the repo rate itself, the RBI sharply raised the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate to squeeze rupee liquidity and defend the currency, an unusual tool choice that this course flags as a reminder that not every yield spike maps cleanly onto the textbook rate-hike story.

events.title: Stabilisation Under a New Governor
events.description: Raghuram Rajan took over as RBI Governor in September 2013 and introduced a special FCNR(B) deposit swap scheme that drew in dollar inflows, helping stabilise the rupee and bring bond yields back down over the following months.

body.text: A sharp bond yield spike is not always the pure growth-expectations signal described in Lesson 2.1. The taper tantrum's yield spike was driven mainly by currency defence and capital flight, an external channel. Before reading a sudden yield move as a recession signal, check whether it is coinciding with rupee weakness and FII outflows, which points to an external, currency-driven cause, or with weakening domestic growth and credit data, which points to the genuine cyclical channel.

children.text: Case Study B: 2018-19, Through the Rate and Policy Lens

Lesson 2.2 covered how credit spreads widened after the IL&FS default in September 2018. This case study adds the piece that lesson left out: what the RBI's own rate and stance were doing at the same time, and how far behind the credit market the RBI's policy pivot actually arrived.

Reported GDP growth confirmed the slowdown, falling toward the 4% range covered in Lesson 1.1, roughly two to three quarters after the credit spread signal first appeared

children.text: The Common Sequence Across Both Episodes

Different triggers, an external currency shock in 2013 and a domestic credit event in 2018, produced a broadly similar sequence: a market-priced signal moved first (bond yields in 2013, credit spreads in 2018), the RBI's own policy stance caught up somewhat later, and reported GDP or IIP data confirmed the slowdown last, generally with a lag of one to three quarters behind the earliest signal. This is the practical payoff of Chapter 2: rather than waiting for any one indicator to cross a threshold, watch for this sequence beginning to unfold across market pricing, RBI communication, and real-economy data together.

body.text: This lesson draws a pattern from exactly two episodes with different underlying causes, one external and one domestic. That is consistent with Lesson 1.3's warning about small samples. Use this sequence as a framework for what to look for, not as a guarantee that the next slowdown will unfold on the same timeline.

body.title: Diagnose the Trigger
body.scenario: Indian G-Sec yields rise sharply over six weeks. At the same time, the rupee has weakened by 6% against the dollar and FII debt outflows have accelerated, while domestic credit growth and PMI new orders have been stable to improving over the same period.
body.prompt: Using the framework from this lesson, is this move more consistent with the 2013 taper-tantrum pattern or the 2018-19 domestic-credit-event pattern, and what would you watch next to confirm your read?
body.modelAnswer: This is far closer to the 2013 pattern: an external, currency-driven yield spike rather than a domestic growth or credit-quality event. The combination of rupee weakness, accelerating FII debt outflows, and yields rising while domestic credit growth and PMI new orders stay stable is the same signature the taper tantrum case study showed, external capital flight pushing yields up for reasons unrelated to the domestic cycle. To confirm, watch whether the RBI responds with currency-defence tools (MSF-style rate actions, FX intervention) rather than a broad-based repo hike, and watch whether credit spreads, particularly for lower-rated domestic borrowers, stay calm; if they do, that further supports an external rather than a domestic credit read.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: In both the 2013 and 2018-19 episodes covered in this lesson, which category of signal arrived last, confirming rather than predicting the slowdown?
options: Market-priced signals, such as bond yields and credit spreads
All three arrived at exactly the same time in both episodes
body.explanation: In both episodes, market pricing moved first, the RBI's stance and rate decisions followed with a lag, and reported GDP and IIP data, both lagging indicators by the classification from Lesson 1.2, confirmed the slowdown last, roughly two to three quarters after the earliest market signal.

body.text: This lesson presents simplified case studies for educational purposes, drawn from widely reported events and approximate, illustrative figures. It is not a complete or precise historical record, and nothing here constitutes investment advice. Always verify specific historical data against RBI and NSE/BSE archives before citing it professionally.

points: The 2013 taper tantrum shows that a sharp yield spike is not always a growth-expectations signal; check for rupee weakness and FII outflows, which point to an external, currency-driven cause instead

The 2018-19 NBFC crisis shows credit spreads widening a full one to two quarters before the RBI's own stance caught up, and GDP data confirming the slowdown roughly two to three quarters after the earliest signal
Different triggers, external in 2013 and domestic in 2018, produced a broadly similar sequence: market pricing first, RBI policy second, real-economy data last
This sequence is drawn from only two clean episodes; treat the specific lag times as an illustrative working prior, not a fixed rule, consistent with Lesson 1.3's small-sample warning
Chapter 3 moves from rate and credit signals to real-economy recession data itself, IIP, PMI, credit growth, and corporate earnings, the data this chapter's signals are meant to lead
